name: Agricultural Drones: Mission Planning and Flight Operations
objectives: Given a client's request for a drone job, write a mission scope with the decision, area, deliverables, dates, contact, price and data sharing, including what the drone cannot do
For a mission site, carry out a desk and ground survey and confirm airspace limits and every permission, recorded with dates and sources before the flight
For a planned mission, write a risk assessment, a flight plan and contingency plans, with a control for every hazard and weather limits set
Before the first flight of a mission, assign crew roles and lead a briefing, covering hazards, limits, contingencies, standard calls and who can call stop
During a mission, monitor the flight and telemetry and make go or no-go decisions, pausing or landing whenever a limit is passed
At the end of a mission, check the data, complete the logs and report any incident, before leaving the site, with gaps reflown and data backed up

lessons.title: Lesson 1: From client request to mission scope
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn a client's request into a clear written mission scope.
This lesson builds toward: Given a client's request for a drone job, you will write a mission scope with the decision, area, deliverables, dates, contact, price and data sharing, including what the drone cannot do.
Clients often ask for "a drone flight" when they need an answer: Which blocks have poor stand? Where is the irrigation leaking? How many trees do we have? Start by asking what decision they want to make and what they will do with the results.
Then agree the scope in writing: the area (with a map or boundary file), the question and the deliverables (for example an orthomosaic, an NDVI map, a tree count, a one-page report), the level of detail needed, the date window, access arrangements, who on the farm is the contact, the price and payment method (such as mobile money on delivery), and how data will be shared and stored.
Say clearly what the drone cannot do. A map can show where trees are stressed; it cannot by itself say which disease it is. A clear scope protects you and the client from disappointment and disputes.
Step by step:
- Ask what decision the client wants to make.
- Agree the area and get a boundary or sketch.
- Agree deliverables, detail, dates and contacts.
- Agree price, payment and data sharing.
- State the limits of what the drone can show.
- Write it down and both confirm.
Words to know:
- Mission scope: the written agreement of what a drone job will cover and deliver.
- Deliverable: a product the client receives, such as a map or report.
Try it now: An avocado exporter says: "Fly our 40 hectares next week." Write five questions you would ask, then write a one-paragraph mission scope with area, deliverables, dates, contact, price placeholder and limits.
You can now turn a vague client request into a clear written mission scope.

check.q: What is a deliverable in a mission scope?
options: The drone's battery
The client's phone number
The flight height
What the client receives, such as a map or a report
check.why: Deliverables are what you hand over, such as an orthomosaic, NDVI map, tree count or report.

check.q: A client wants your NDVI map to name the disease in their avocados. What do you write in the scope?
options: That the map will name every disease
That the map shows stressed trees, but a disease needs to be identified on the ground
Nothing about it
That you will spray the trees too
check.why: A map can show where trees are stressed but cannot by itself say which disease it is.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Site survey, airspace and permissions
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Survey a site and confirm airspace limits and every permission before the flight.
This lesson builds toward: For a mission site, you will carry out a desk and ground survey and confirm airspace limits and every permission, recorded with dates and sources before the flight.
Do a desk survey first: look at the area on a map app and satellite view for airstrips, airports, roads, towns, power lines, masts, rivers, protected areas and security sites. Then check your authority's rules and maps for restricted areas and aerodrome distances, and whether the job needs a specific operation authorisation. Allow time for any approval to come through.
Then survey on the ground if you can, or ask the farm contact for photos: take-off and landing spots, obstacles and their heights, people and animals, homesteads, access roads, mobile network coverage, and where the crew can shelter from sun and rain.
Confirm permissions: the landowner or manager in writing, neighbours if you will cross their land, any community leaders where that is expected, and the aviation authority as required. Record everything in the mission pack with dates and sources.
Step by step:
- Desk survey: map and satellite view of the area.
- Check aviation rules: restricted areas, aerodrome distances, authorisations.
- Ground survey or farm photos: take-off spots, obstacles, people, network.
- Get landowner and neighbour permissions in writing.
- Record all checks with dates and sources.
Words to know:
- Desk survey: checking a site using maps and documents before going there.
- Restricted area: airspace where flying is limited or needs special permission.
- Operation authorisation: permission from the aviation authority for a particular kind of operation.
Official sources:
- Kenya Civil Aviation Authority (KCAA): Unmanned Aircraft Systems
- KCAA drone (RPAS) online system
- Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA): Nig.CARs 2023 Part 21, Remotely Piloted Aircraft Systems
Try it now: For a farm you can find on a map app, do a desk survey: list every airstrip, road, power line, settlement and protected area within a few kilometres, and write which aviation rules you must check and which permissions you need.
You can now survey a site, check airspace limits and secure every permission before a mission.

options: A meeting at the client's desk
Flying a test flight
Looking at maps and satellite views for hazards and restricted areas before going to the site
Counting the crew
check.why: A desk survey checks maps, satellite views and the authority's rules before the site visit.

check.q: Your flight lines will cross a neighbour's land. What do you do before the flight?
options: Get the neighbour's permission and record it in the mission pack
Fly high so they do not notice
Fly only early in the morning
Ask the client to tell them afterwards
check.why: Permissions from landowners and neighbours are confirmed and recorded before the flight.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Risk assessment and the flight plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a risk assessment and a complete flight plan with contingencies.
This lesson builds toward: For a planned mission, you will write a risk assessment, a flight plan and contingency plans, with a control for every hazard and weather limits set.
A risk assessment lists what could go wrong, how likely and how serious it is, and what you will do to reduce it. For example: hazard, a power line along the north boundary; risk, collision; control, plan lines 30 m away and set return-to-home above it. Other common hazards: people walking into the area, livestock, birds of prey, strong afternoon winds, heat, lost link behind hills, and an airstrip nearby.
The flight plan sets: the area split into flights that each fit one battery; height and the image detail it gives (within the legal height limit); overlap; speed; the number of batteries, with spares; take-off and landing points; the time window (for example 10:00 to 14:00 for even light); and weather limits (maximum wind, no rain, visibility). Check the forecast from your national weather service the day before and the morning of the job.
Contingencies say what you will do if things change: wind above your limit, so pause; rain, so pack up and come back on the reserve date; a person enters the area, so hold or land; lost link, so return-to-home is set; a battery fault, so land at the alternate landing point.
Step by step:
- List hazards; rate likelihood and severity; write a control for each.
- Split the area into one-battery flights.
- Set height, detail, overlap, speed and batteries with spares.
- Set time window and weather limits; check the forecast.
- Write contingencies and alternate landing points.
Words to know:
- Risk assessment: a written check of what could go wrong and how you will reduce the risk.
- Control: an action that reduces a risk.
- Contingency: a pre-planned action if something changes or goes wrong.
Official sources:
- Kenya Meteorological Department
- Nigerian Meteorological Agency (NiMet)
- Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA): Nig.CARs 2023 Part 21, Remotely Piloted Aircraft Systems
Try it now: Write a risk assessment table with at least six hazards for the 40-hectare avocado job, then write its flight plan and five contingencies.
You can now write a risk assessment and a complete flight plan with contingencies.

check.q: In a risk assessment, what is a hazard?
options: Something that could cause harm, such as a power line
The client's payment
The flight's deliverable
The drone's colour
check.why: A hazard is what could go wrong; the risk assessment adds likelihood, severity and a control.

check.q: Your plan sets a maximum wind. The morning forecast shows wind above it all day. What do you do?
options: Fly anyway and hope
Remove the wind limit from the plan
Fly only the far side of the farm
Use the reserve date in the contingency plan
check.why: Contingencies say what to do when conditions pass a limit, such as coming back on the reserve date.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Crew roles and the briefing
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Assign crew roles and lead a clear pre-mission briefing.
This lesson builds toward: Before the first flight of a mission, you will assign crew roles and lead a briefing, covering hazards, limits, contingencies, standard calls and who can call stop.
Even small missions go better with clear roles. The remote pilot in command is responsible for the safety of the flight and has the final say. The observer watches the drone and the sky and warns of aircraft, birds, people and animals. A ground or payload operator may manage batteries, the camera, the landing area and the client.
Before the first flight, the pilot in command briefs everyone, including the farm contact: the area and flight lines, height, time on each battery, take-off and landing points, hazards and controls from the risk assessment, weather limits, the contingency plans, the words you will use (for example "hold", "land now"), and who can call a stop. Anyone can call stop for safety.
Check that each crew member has water, sun protection and safety gear such as high-visibility vests, and that the take-off area is marked and kept clear of onlookers.
Step by step:
- Assign pilot in command, observer and ground or payload operator.
- Brief: area, height, batteries, take-off and landing, hazards, weather limits.
- Agree contingencies and standard calls (hold, land now).
- Confirm anyone can call stop.
- Mark the take-off area; check water, sun protection and vests.
Words to know:
- Pilot in command: the remote pilot responsible for the safety of the flight, with the final say.
- Standard calls: short, agreed words the crew uses so everyone understands at once.
Try it now: Write a one-page briefing script for the avocado mission that a pilot in command could read out in three minutes, covering every item from this lesson.
You can now assign crew roles and lead a clear pre-mission briefing.

options: Pays the crew
Watches the drone, the sky and the ground and warns the pilot
Writes the client's report
Charges the client
check.why: The observer watches for aircraft, birds, people and animals and warns the pilot.

check.q: The farm contact will stand near the take-off area. What do you do in the briefing?
options: Leave them out of the briefing
Tell them to stay quiet
Include them, explain the hazards and the standard calls, and tell them anyone can call stop
Ask them to fly the drone
check.why: The briefing includes everyone on site, including the farm contact, and anyone can call stop for safety.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Executing and monitoring the mission
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Fly a planned mission, monitor it and make go or no-go decisions.
This lesson builds toward: During a mission, you will monitor the flight and telemetry and make go or no-go decisions, pausing or landing whenever a limit is passed.
Before each flight, run the pre-flight checklist and confirm the conditions are within limits. Upload or check the planned route, confirm the home point and return-to-home height, and confirm the observer is in position.
During the flight, the pilot watches the drone and the telemetry (battery, signal, satellites, wind warnings, height, progress along the lines). The observer watches the sky and the ground. Be ready to take manual control at any moment. Swap batteries between flights following your battery procedure, and mark which lines are done.
Make go or no-go decisions all day. If the wind rises above your limit, a person walks into the area, a storm builds, or a warning repeats, pause or land. Finishing tomorrow is better than an accident today. Keep the client informed of progress and any changes.
Step by step:
- Pre-flight checklist; conditions within limits?
- Check route, home point and return-to-home height.
- Fly; pilot watches drone and telemetry, observer watches sky and ground.
- Swap batteries safely; mark completed lines.
- Pause or land if limits are exceeded; tell the client.
Words to know:
- Telemetry: live data the drone sends to the controller: battery, height, position, signal, warnings.
- Go / no-go: the decision whether it is safe to fly or continue.
Official sources:
- Kenya Civil Aviation Authority (KCAA): Unmanned Aircraft Systems
- Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA): Nig.CARs 2023 Part 21, Remotely Piloted Aircraft Systems
Try it now: Write a go / no-go card for your mission: five conditions that mean go, and five that mean stop or land, in short words a crew could read in the field.
You can now fly and monitor a planned mission and make sound go or no-go decisions.

options: The client's contract
The weather forecast
Live flight data such as battery, height, signal and warnings
The crew roster
check.why: Telemetry is the live data the pilot watches during the flight.

check.q: A storm is building and half the lines are done. What do you do?
options: Land, and finish the rest later
Fly faster to finish
Turn off the warnings
Let the observer fly while you pack
check.why: Finishing tomorrow is better than an accident today; pause or land when conditions become unsafe.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Closing the mission: data checks, logs and incidents
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Check data, complete logs and handle incident reports before leaving the site.
This lesson builds toward: At the end of a mission, you will check the data, complete the logs and report any incident, before leaving the site, with gaps reflown and data backed up.
Before you leave the site, check the data: count the images per flight, look at a sample for blur and exposure, check for gaps in coverage, and if possible run a quick low-resolution stitch on a laptop. Refly any gaps while the crew and conditions are there. Back up the data to a second device.
Complete the records: flight logs for each flight (time, battery, pilot, problems), battery and maintenance notes, and the mission pack's actual conditions. Thank the farm contact and confirm when they will receive the deliverables.
If anything went wrong (a crash, a near miss with an aircraft, injury, damage to property, a fly-away), make the area safe first, then record what happened and report it to your aviation authority as its rules require, and to your insurer. Review the incident with the crew and update your procedures so it does not happen again.
Step by step:
- Count images, sample for blur, check coverage gaps.
- Refly gaps; back up data to a second device.
- Complete flight, battery and maintenance logs.
- Confirm delivery date with the client.
- For any incident: make safe, record, report as required, review and update procedures.
Words to know:
- Near miss: an event where an accident almost happened.
- Coverage gap: an area with missing or poor images.
Official sources:
- Kenya Civil Aviation Authority (KCAA): Unmanned Aircraft Systems
- Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA): Nig.CARs 2023 Part 21, Remotely Piloted Aircraft Systems
Try it now: Final task: assemble your complete mission pack: scope, site survey and sketch map, airspace and permission checks with sources, risk assessment, flight plan, crew roles and briefing, contingencies, go / no-go card, and the post-flight checklist and log template.
You can now close a mission professionally with data checks, complete logs and correct incident handling.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Mission scope The client's decision, area or deliverables are missing. Decision, area, deliverables, detail, dates, contact, price and data sharing are written, with what the drone cannot do. Signed or confirmed in writing by the client. Site survey and permissions No survey, or permissions and airspace checks are missing. Desk and ground survey with a sketch map of hazards, airspace checks with sources, and written permissions. Includes network coverage, crew shelter and dates for every check. Risk assessment Hazards are listed without controls. A table with hazard, likelihood, severity and control for each main hazard. Covers heat, wind, onlookers, lost link and any nearby airstrip. Flight plan and contingencies Height, overlap, batteries or weather limits are missing. Area split into flights, height, image detail, overlap, speed, batteries with spares, timing, weather limits and contingencies. Shows the battery count worked out and a reserve date. Crew and briefing No roles or briefing notes. Named roles and briefing notes with hazards, limits, contingencies and standard calls. Includes safety gear, water and how onlookers are kept clear. Closing the mission No post-flight checklist or log. A post-flight checklist with data checks, backups, flight logs and the incident reporting steps. Includes how lessons from incidents update the procedures. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part of the pack and check it again.

check.q: What is a quick low-resolution stitch for?
options: Making the final report
Charging batteries
Sending the invoice
Checking for gaps in coverage before leaving the site
check.why: A quick stitch shows gaps while the crew and conditions are still there to refly them.

check.q: Your drone hit a fence post and broke a propeller. What do you do first?
options: Report it next month
Make the area safe, then record it and report it as the rules require
Hide the damage from the client
Fly the next mission with the same propeller
check.why: Make the area safe first, then record the incident and report it to the authority and insurer as required.
